title: Earth's Features & Water Cycle
description: The water cycle moves water between Earth's surface and atmosphere through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. Earth has diverse land and water features.

exercises.question: What are the main steps of the WATER CYCLE in order?
exercises.exp: Water evaporates (rises), condenses into clouds, then falls as precipitation (rain/snow) — the cycle repeats!

exercises.question: What is EVAPORATION in the water cycle?
choices: liquid water turning into water vapour and rising
exercises.exp: Evaporation is when the sun heats water on Earth's surface, turning it into water vapour that rises into the sky.

exercises.question: What is CONDENSATION in the water cycle?
choices: water vapour cooling and turning into tiny water droplets (forming clouds)
exercises.exp: When water vapour rises high and cools down, it condenses into tiny water droplets — forming clouds!

exercises.question: What is PRECIPITATION?
choices: any water that falls from clouds to the ground (rain, snow, sleet)
exercises.exp: Precipitation is water falling from clouds — as rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on temperature.

exercises.question: Where does most of Earth's FRESH WATER come from?
exercises.exp: Most fresh water is locked in glaciers and ice caps. A small amount is in rivers, lakes, and groundwater.

exercises.question: What percentage of Earth's water is FRESH (not salty)?
exercises.exp: Only about 3% of Earth's water is fresh — and most of that is frozen in glaciers. Very little is drinkable!

exercises.question: Which is a RENEWABLE natural resource?
exercises.exp: Water is renewed through the water cycle — evaporation and precipitation constantly recycle it!

exercises.question: What is a GLACIER?
choices: a large, slow-moving mass of ice
exercises.exp: Glaciers are massive bodies of ice that move slowly. They store huge amounts of fresh water and shape the land.

exercises.question: When does RUNOFF occur in the water cycle?
choices: when precipitation flows across the land surface into streams and rivers
when clouds form in the sky
when water soaks deep into the ground
exercises.exp: Runoff is precipitation that cannot soak into the ground — it flows across the surface into streams and rivers.

exercises.question: What is GROUNDWATER?
choices: water stored underground in rock and soil
water in the air as vapour
exercises.exp: Groundwater is water that has soaked into the ground and is stored in gaps in rocks and soil. We pump it up through wells!

exercises.question: Which is NOT a natural land feature?
exercises.exp: A highway is built by humans — it is not a natural land feature. Canyons, peninsulas, and deltas are all natural.

exercises.question: A DELTA forms where ___.
choices: a river meets a larger body of water and deposits sediment
exercises.exp: Where a river slows as it meets a lake or ocean, it deposits sediment that fans out to form a delta.

exercises.question: Where does MOST of Earth's fresh water exist?
choices: locked in glaciers and ice caps (about 69% of all fresh water)
exercises.exp: Almost 69% of Earth's fresh water is frozen in glaciers and ice sheets. Less than 1% is in accessible rivers, lakes, and groundwater!

exercises.question: What is the WATER TABLE?
choices: a table shaped by water erosion
the upper surface of underground water-saturated rock and soil (groundwater)
the level of a lake or river
the boundary between ocean and land
exercises.exp: The water table is the top of the underground zone where all spaces are filled with water. Dig below it — you find groundwater!

exercises.question: SPRINGS occur where ___.
choices: groundwater naturally flows to the surface where the water table meets the land
rainfall collects in bowls in the land
exercises.exp: Springs form where the water table intersects the surface — groundwater bubbles up naturally. They are important sources of clean fresh water!

exercises.question: What drives the WATER CYCLE?
choices: energy from the sun (drives evaporation) and gravity (drives precipitation and runoff)
exercises.exp: The sun provides energy for evaporation (lifting water). Gravity pulls precipitation and runoff back down. Together they power the endless water cycle!

exercises.question: INFILTRATION in the water cycle is when ___.
choices: water soaks into the ground, replenishing groundwater aquifers
water runs across the surface in streams
exercises.exp: Infiltration: water seeps through soil and rock into underground aquifers. Forests and permeable soil allow high infiltration; pavement blocks it — causing flooding!

exercises.question: Canada's GREAT LAKES hold about 21% of the world's SURFACE FRESH WATER. Why is this significant?
choices: it means Canada never has water shortages
the Great Lakes are an enormous, irreplaceable fresh water resource — vital for millions of people, agriculture, and ecosystems in Canada and the US
only people near the lakes can use the water
the lakes will be used up within 50 years
exercises.exp: The Great Lakes system is the world's largest group of freshwater lakes by total area — supplying drinking water to 40+ million people and supporting enormous biodiversity.

exercises.question: AQUIFERS are underground layers of permeable rock or sediment that hold water. Why are they important?
choices: they are only used by farmers
they supply groundwater for wells and springs — providing fresh water to millions of people in areas without surface water
aquifers are always visible from the surface
exercises.exp: Aquifers are underground freshwater reserves — many cities and farms depend on pumping aquifer water. They recharge slowly, so overuse is a serious sustainability concern.

exercises.question: TRANSPIRATION by plants contributes to the water cycle by ___.
choices: releasing water vapour from leaves into the atmosphere, contributing to precipitation
exercises.exp: Plants absorb groundwater and release it as water vapour through leaves — a process called transpiration. Forests release enormous amounts of water, seeding rain clouds.

exercises.question: A WATERSHED (or drainage basin) is ___.
choices: the entire area of land that drains into a particular river or lake
only the land next to a river
exercises.exp: A watershed is all the land where rain and snow drain toward a common outlet — a river, lake, or ocean. The Great Lakes watershed covers over 500,000 km²!

exercises.question: Why is the OCEAN SALTY but lakes and rivers are FRESH?
choices: all bodies of water are equally salty
rivers carry small amounts of dissolved minerals to the ocean — which never drains so salts accumulate over millions of years; rivers and lakes continuously flush out and cycle water
the sun adds salt to the ocean
exercises.exp: Rivers dissolve tiny amounts of salt from rock and carry it to the ocean. The ocean has no outlet — water evaporates (leaving salt behind) but salt stays and accumulates over billions of years!

exercises.question: POLLUTION of a RIVER affects ecosystems DOWNSTREAM. Why?
choices: water only flows sideways, not downstream
rivers carry pollutants with the current — affecting every ecosystem the water flows through, often far from the pollution source
exercises.exp: Rivers are connected systems — a spill upstream travels downstream, affecting all the ecosystems, towns, and wildlife that depend on that water. We share rivers with everyone downstream!

exercises.question: The HYDROSPHERE refers to ___.
choices: ALL water on, above, and within Earth — oceans, lakes, rivers, ice, groundwater, and atmospheric water
exercises.exp: The hydrosphere includes ALL water on Earth in any form — salty ocean, fresh lakes, glaciers, rivers, groundwater, and water vapour in the atmosphere.

exercises.question: EROSION and DEPOSITION work TOGETHER. What is the relationship?
choices: they cancel each other out and nothing changes
erosion breaks down and removes material; deposition drops it in a new place — together they build and destroy landforms
exercises.exp: Erosion removes material (wearing down mountains and coastlines). Deposition drops it elsewhere (building deltas, beaches, and plains). Material moves — it is just rearranged!

exercises.question: A DAM on a river creates a reservoir (artificial lake). How does this affect the water cycle?
choices: dams prevent the water cycle from operating
dams increase evaporation from the large reservoir surface and alter natural water flow, sediment transport, and downstream water availability
dams have no effect on the water cycle
dams purify water so it evaporates more cleanly
exercises.exp: Dams create large water surfaces (more evaporation), trap sediment behind the dam (starving downstream areas), alter flow timing, and affect fish migration — major water cycle changes!

exercises.question: CANADA has the most LAKES of any country. Why are healthy lakes important?
choices: they store fresh water, regulate climate, support biodiversity, provide drinking water, and are culturally important to Indigenous communities
lakes are only useful for generating electricity
lakes make the land more beautiful
exercises.exp: Canada's 2+ million lakes store enormous amounts of fresh water, support rich aquatic ecosystems, moderate regional climate, and are deeply tied to Indigenous culture and identity.

exercises.question: When GLACIERS MELT due to climate change, what happens to sea levels?
choices: sea levels decrease as water is absorbed by land
sea levels rise — the extra melt water flows into the ocean
glaciers do not contain enough water to affect sea level
exercises.exp: Glaciers and ice sheets hold enormous amounts of water. As they melt, that water flows into oceans — raising sea levels globally, threatening coastal communities!

exercises.question: PERMAFROST is permanently frozen ground found in northern Canada and the Arctic. What happens when permafrost THAWS due to warming?
choices: thawing permafrost becomes unstable, releasing stored carbon (methane and CO₂), damaging infrastructure, and altering wetland ecosystems
thawing permafrost creates new lakes permanently
exercises.exp: Permafrost stores vast amounts of ancient carbon. As it thaws, it releases methane and CO₂, amplifying climate change — a feedback loop. It also damages buildings and roads built on it!

exercises.question: The AMAZON RAINFOREST is sometimes called the 'lungs of the Earth'. Why?
choices: it absorbs enormous amounts of CO₂ and produces oxygen through photosynthesis — and releases vast amounts of water vapour that seed rain across South America
its trees look like lung tissue
the Amazon makes Earth breathe faster
exercises.exp: The Amazon's billions of trees photosynthesize massively (absorbing CO₂, producing O₂) and transpire so much water they create their own rain — 'flying rivers' of moisture!

exercises.question: What is DESALINATION?
choices: the process of removing salt from seawater to produce fresh drinking water
exercises.exp: Desalination makes fresh water from seawater — important for water-scarce countries. It is energy-intensive but becoming more affordable and common as fresh water becomes scarcer.

exercises.question: Earth's layers from outside to inside are ___.
choices: mantle, crust, outer core, inner core
crust, mantle, outer core, inner core
outer core, inner core, mantle, crust
exercises.exp: Earth: crust (thin outer rock), mantle (thick, slowly flowing rock), outer core (liquid iron-nickel), inner core (solid iron-nickel). The inner core is hottest!

exercises.question: What is the ASTHENOSPHERE?
choices: the outermost layer of the atmosphere
the partly molten, plastic-like upper mantle on which tectonic plates float and move
the boundary between inner and outer core
exercises.exp: The asthenosphere is the zone in the upper mantle where rock is hot enough to flow very slowly. Tectonic plates 'float' on it and are driven by convection currents within it.

exercises.question: PLATE TECTONICS explains that ___.
choices: Earth's surface has always been in its current configuration
Earth's lithosphere is broken into plates that move, driven by heat from Earth's interior — causing earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain building
mountains grow upward permanently without limits
exercises.exp: Plate tectonics unified geology. Plate movement explains: earthquake distribution, volcanic zones, mountain formation, and how continents drifted from Pangaea to current positions!

exercises.question: SUBDUCTION occurs when ___.
choices: one tectonic plate dives beneath another into the mantle, melting and often producing volcanoes above
two plates slide past each other
plates stop moving due to friction
exercises.exp: Subduction: denser oceanic plates dive under less dense continental plates. The subducting plate melts, producing magma that rises to form volcanic mountain chains!

exercises.question: The MID-ATLANTIC RIDGE is an example of a ___.
choices: divergent boundary — plates moving APART with new ocean floor forming in between
exercises.exp: Divergent boundaries: plates move apart, magma wells up, creating new ocean floor. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge grows about 2.5 cm per year — Iceland sits right on it!

exercises.question: TRANSFORM FAULT boundaries (like the San Andreas Fault) are where plates ___.
choices: slide past each other horizontally — causing earthquakes but not volcanoes
one plate subducts under the other
exercises.exp: Transform boundaries: plates grind past each other → earthquakes (no volcanism). The San Andreas Fault (California) is a famous transform boundary where the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other.

exercises.question: The ROCK CYCLE shows ___.
choices: that rocks always stay in the same form
how the three rock types (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic) can each transform into the others through geological processes over time
that only sedimentary rocks contain fossils
exercises.exp: Rock cycle: igneous rocks weather → sedimentary rocks form → with heat/pressure → metamorphic rocks form → if melted → magma cools → igneous rocks again. All rock types interconnect!

exercises.question: METAMORPHIC rocks are formed by ___.
choices: existing rocks being transformed by high heat and/or pressure deep in Earth's crust (without melting)
exercises.exp: Metamorphic means 'changed form.' Limestone heated and pressured becomes marble; shale becomes slate; granite becomes gneiss. New mineral structures form without melting!

exercises.question: SOIL FORMATION (pedogenesis) takes ___.
choices: decades to centuries for young soils; thousands to millions of years for deep fertile soils
soil forms instantly when rock crumbles
exercises.exp: Soil forms incredibly slowly — about 1 cm of topsoil takes 200-1000 years to form from weathered rock + organic matter. Erosion can remove a lifetime of soil in one storm!

exercises.question: GLACIERS are agents of erosion. They create characteristic ___.
choices: horizontal flat plains by compressing rock
U-shaped valleys — their enormous mass scours and carves the rock into wide, flat-bottomed valley shapes
exercises.exp: Glaciers are so massive and slow that they scour valleys into U-shapes (valleys formed by rivers are V-shaped). Yosemite Valley and Norwegian fjords show classic glacial U-shapes!

exercises.question: The HYDROSPHERE includes ___.
choices: all water on, above, and below Earth's surface — oceans, lakes, rivers, glaciers, groundwater, and atmospheric water vapour
only frozen water at the poles
exercises.exp: The hydrosphere is ALL of Earth's water in all forms and locations. 97% is in the oceans (saltwater); 3% is fresh (most frozen as ice). Only 0.3% is accessible liquid fresh water!

exercises.question: CHEMICAL WEATHERING breaks down rock by ___.
choices: chemical reactions (oxidation, acid reactions, hydrolysis) that change the mineral composition of rock
exercises.exp: Chemical weathering: acid rain dissolves limestone (karst landscapes); oxygen rusts iron minerals; water reacts with feldspar to form clay. Rock composition changes chemically!

exercises.question: PHYSICAL WEATHERING breaks down rock WITHOUT changing its composition. Which is an example?
choices: iron in rock oxidising to rust
freeze-thaw: water freezes in cracks, expands, widens cracks until rock breaks
acid from lichens dissolving rock surface
exercises.exp: Freeze-thaw weathering: water seeps into cracks, freezes (expands 9%), forces cracks wider, then thaws. Repeated cycles break rock into smaller pieces with same mineral composition.

exercises.question: The CARBON CYCLE involves rocks. How does CARBON get stored in sedimentary rock?
choices: rocks absorb CO₂ from the air directly
atmospheric CO₂ dissolves in rainwater (forming carbonic acid) → reacts with rock → bicarbonate washed to ocean → marine organisms use it for shells → shells become limestone
glaciers freeze CO₂ into ice sheets
exercises.exp: CO₂ → carbonic acid → dissolves silicate rocks → washed to ocean → marine life uses calcium carbonate for shells → shells accumulate on seafloor → compressed into limestone. Geological carbon storage!

exercises.question: AQUIFERS are ___.
choices: underground layers of permeable rock or sediment saturated with groundwater — a major source of fresh water
the water in deep ocean trenches
exercises.exp: Aquifers store enormous amounts of groundwater in porous rock like sandstone and gravel. Wells tap into aquifers — billions of people depend on groundwater!

exercises.question: Why is TOPSOIL the most important layer of soil for agriculture?
choices: it is the oldest and most compressed layer
it contains the most rocks for nutrients
it is richest in organic matter and microorganisms — directly supporting plant growth and food production
exercises.exp: Topsoil = humus-rich layer containing nutrients, microbes, and organic matter. Without topsoil, agriculture fails. It takes centuries to form and can erode in decades — precious resource!

exercises.question: ISOSTASY is the principle that ___.
choices: Earth's crust floats on the mantle — adding mass pushes it down; removing mass allows it to rise (like ice melting allows the land to rise)
all continents are moving toward each other
tectonic plates are all moving at the same speed
exercises.exp: Isostasy: like a loaded ship sinks deeper, heavy ice sheets push crust into mantle. When ice melts, crust slowly rises (isostatic rebound). Scandinavia is still rising from Ice Age glacier removal!

exercises.question: What is the age of the Earth, estimated by radiometric dating?
exercises.exp: Radiometric dating of ancient zircon crystals gives Earth's age as 4.54 billion years. The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.
